orbit: The closed path a body follows around another under gravity — an ellipse in the simplest case.
trajectory: The path a spacecraft follows through space, open or closed — for example the arc from Earth to Mars.
inclination: The tilt of an orbit's plane against a reference plane, such as Earth's equator or the ecliptic, in degrees.
rendezvous: Bringing two spacecraft to the same place at the same speed so that they fly together — usually the step before docking.
docking: Joining two spacecraft mechanically so that crew or cargo can pass between them.
gravity assist: Using a close pass of a planet to change a spacecraft's speed and direction without spending propellant.
delta-v: Change in velocity, written Δv: how much a spacecraft can change its motion, the currency of every mission plan, in km/s.
apogee: The point of an orbit around Earth that is farthest from Earth.
perigee: The point of an orbit around Earth that is closest to Earth.
burn: A period of firing a rocket engine to change a spacecraft's velocity.
stage: A section of a rocket with its own engines and propellant, dropped when its propellant is used up.
propellant: What a rocket engine uses up to make thrust: usually a fuel and an oxidizer together.
payload: What a rocket carries for the mission: satellites, a crewed spacecraft, cargo or instruments.
thrust: The force a rocket engine produces to push the vehicle forward, measured in newtons.
booster: A rocket that provides thrust at launch: a first stage, or a strap-on rocket at the side of the core.
specific impulse: How efficiently an engine uses its propellant, in seconds: the higher it is, the more Δv from the same propellant.
flyby: A close pass by a planet, moon or other body without going into orbit around it or landing.
orbit insertion: The engine burn that slows a spacecraft enough to be captured into orbit around its destination.
entry: A spacecraft's passage into a planet's atmosphere, where drag and heating slow it down.
descent: The way down to a surface, from orbit or from the atmosphere to touchdown.
orbiter: A spacecraft that goes into orbit around a planet, moon or other body to study it from above, often for years.
lander: A spacecraft that sets down on the surface of a planet, moon or small body and works where it lands.
rover: A vehicle that drives across the surface of another world, carrying its instruments from place to place.
capsule: The part of a spacecraft that brings the crew or the cargo home through the atmosphere, protected by a heat shield.
upper stage: The top stage of a rocket, which finishes the climb to orbit or sends the payload on towards its destination.
heat shield: The layer that protects a spacecraft from the heat of atmospheric entry, usually by charring and wearing away.
airlock: A small chamber between a spacecraft's pressurised cabin and the vacuum outside, emptied and refilled with air so that crews can go out and come back in.
spacewalk: Work done by an astronaut outside a spacecraft, in a spacesuit; also called EVA (extravehicular activity).
splashdown: The end of a flight home in which a capsule comes down in the sea under parachutes and is picked up by a recovery ship.
sample return: Collecting material on another world and bringing it back to Earth, where laboratories can study it far more closely than any instrument sent there.
regolith: The layer of loose, broken rock and dust that covers the Moon, Mars and asteroids, ground up by billions of years of impacts.
microgravity: The near-weightless state of everything in orbit, which is falling around the Earth together with its spacecraft.
life support: The systems that keep a crew alive: breathable air, water, the right temperature and the removal of carbon dioxide and waste.
solar array: The panels of solar cells that turn sunlight into electricity for a spacecraft or a station.
low Earth orbit: An orbit from about 160 to 2,000 km above the Earth, where the ISS and most satellites fly, circling the planet in about 90 minutes.
geostationary: The circular orbit 35,786 km above the equator in which a satellite goes round once a day and so stays over the same spot on the ground.
polar orbit: An orbit that passes over or near both poles, so the ground turns beneath it and the spacecraft sees the whole surface in time.
perihelion: The point of an orbit around the Sun that is closest to the Sun.
aphelion: The point of an orbit around the Sun that is farthest from the Sun.
eccentricity: How stretched an orbit is: 0 is a circle, values between 0 and 1 are ever longer ellipses, 1 and above are open paths that never return.
launch window: The period in which a launch can reach its target with the propellant on board, set by where the Earth and the target are.
escape velocity: The speed an object needs to leave a body for good without further thrust: about 11.2 km/s from the Earth's surface.
Hohmann transfer: The cheapest way between two circular orbits: one burn onto half an ellipse that touches both, and a second burn to circularise at the far end.
Lagrange point: One of five points where the pull of two large bodies and the motion of orbit balance, so a small object can keep its place relative to both.
C3: Characteristic energy: the square of the speed left over once a spacecraft has escaped the Earth, in km²/s² — the figure a launcher must reach for a given trip.
rocket equation: Tsiolkovsky's equation, Δv = vₑ · ln(m₀/m₁): the change in speed a rocket can make from its exhaust velocity and how much of its mass is propellant.
free-return: A path to the Moon that swings round its far side and falls back to Earth with no further burn, so a crew can come home even if the engine fails.
sun-synchronous: A near-polar orbit whose plane turns with the Earth's yearly path, so the satellite crosses each latitude at the same local solar time every day.
halo orbit: A looping orbit around a Lagrange point, held there by the balance of two bodies' gravity — JWST circles one at L2, Gateway was planned for another.
exoplanet: A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun; more than 5,000 are known, most found by the dip in light as they cross their star.
light-year: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km — a measure of distance, not of time.
habitable zone: The range of distances from a star where a planet could keep liquid water on its surface: not too hot, not too cold.
asteroid belt: The wide ring of rocky and metallic bodies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, so thinly spread that spacecraft cross it without trouble.
solar wind: The stream of charged particles that flows out from the Sun in every direction at hundreds of kilometres per second.
magnetosphere: The region around a planet ruled by its magnetic field, which turns the solar wind aside and traps charged particles in belts.
observatory: A place on the ground where telescopes and antennas watch the sky — optical domes, radio dishes, deep-space antennas.
black hole: A region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it has crossed the event horizon.
supermassive black hole: A black hole of millions to billions of solar masses, found at the centre of nearly all large galaxies, the Milky Way included.
stellar-mass black hole: A black hole of a few to a few tens of solar masses, formed when a massive star collapses at the end of its life.
event horizon: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can return, light included.
accretion disk: The flat swirl of gas that spirals in towards a compact object such as a black hole, heating up and glowing as it falls.
black hole shadow: The dark patch at the centre of the glowing gas around a black hole: the closest we can come to an image of the black hole itself, and larger than its event horizon because gravity bends the light around it.
gravitational lensing: The bending of light by gravity: a massive object between us and a distant source warps the path of its light and distorts, magnifies or multiplies its image.
supernova: The explosion of a star at the end of its life, bright enough to briefly rival a whole galaxy; the core may be left behind as a neutron star or a black hole.
general relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity: mass and energy curve space and time, and that curvature is what we experience as gravity.
Doppler effect: The change in the frequency of light or sound when its source moves towards or away from the observer: higher when approaching, lower when receding.
active galactic nucleus: The extremely bright centre of a galaxy, powered by gas falling onto a supermassive black hole; in the brightest cases it outshines all the galaxy's stars put together.
apparent magnitude: How bright an object looks from Earth, on a scale where a smaller number means a brighter object; under dark skies the faintest stars seen with the unaided eye are about magnitude 6.
asterism: A recognisable pattern of stars that is not an official constellation, such as the Big Dipper.
barred spiral galaxy: A spiral galaxy with a bar of stars, gas and dust cutting straight across its centre.
binary star: Two stars bound by gravity that orbit a common centre of mass; their orbits let astronomers weigh them.
blueshift: The shift of light towards shorter, bluer wavelengths when its source is moving towards the observer.
blue straggler: A star in a cluster that looks hotter and younger than its neighbours; thought to form when two stars merge or one pulls gas from a companion.
brown dwarf: An object more massive than a planet but too light to fuse hydrogen in its core the way a star does.
Cepheid variable: A pulsating star whose brightness rises and falls in a regular cycle; the longer the cycle, the brighter the star, which makes Cepheids a yardstick for distance.
dark matter: Matter that gives off no light and has so far been detected only through its gravity; it makes up most of the matter in the universe, but what it is made of is still unknown.
dark nebula: A cloud of gas and dust so thick that it blocks the light of the stars and glowing gas behind it.
dwarf galaxy: A small, faint galaxy; the most common kind, often found as a companion to a larger galaxy.
elliptical galaxy: A galaxy whose stars form a smooth round-to-oval ball rather than a flat disk with arms.
emission nebula: A cloud of gas that glows with its own light because ultraviolet light from nearby hot, young stars energises it.
galaxy cluster: A group of hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound together by their own gravity.
galaxy group: A smaller gathering of galaxies bound by gravity, usually fewer than about 50; the Milky Way belongs to the Local Group.
globular cluster: A large, tightly packed, roughly spherical ball of old stars.
gravitational microlensing: The brief brightening of a distant star when a nearer object passes almost exactly in front of it and its gravity acts as a lens; it can reveal objects, planets included, that give off little or no light.
intermediate-mass black hole: A black hole of roughly a hundred to hundreds of thousands of solar masses, between the stellar-mass and supermassive kinds; candidates exist but few are confirmed.
lenticular galaxy: A galaxy with the central bulge and flat disk of a spiral but no spiral arms.
light echo: Light from a bright flash, such as a supernova, that reaches us late because it was scattered off a dust cloud along a longer path.
maser: A natural source of intense microwave radio emission, the radio counterpart of a laser, found in star-forming clouds, around old stars and near some galactic centres.
Messier catalogue: A list of 110 star clusters, nebulae and galaxies, begun by Charles Messier in the 1700s so that comet hunters would not mistake them for comets.
molecular cloud: A cold, dense cloud of gas and dust, mostly hydrogen molecules, in which stars are born.
nebula: A cloud of gas and dust in space; some are birthplaces of stars, others the remains of dying ones.
neutron star: The collapsed core of a massive star left after a supernova: more than the Sun's mass packed into a ball about the size of a city.
nova: A sudden outburst in which a white dwarf in a close pair pulls gas from its companion until the gas ignites on its surface, brightening the system by thousands of times or more before it fades over weeks to months.
open cluster: A loose group of tens to thousands of stars that formed together from one gas cloud, found in a galaxy's disk, like the Pleiades.
parallax: The apparent shift of a nearby object against the distant background when the viewpoint changes; for stars, Earth's yearly orbit gives the shift that measures their distance.
planetary nebula: A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying low- or medium-mass star, leaving a white dwarf at its centre; the name comes from early telescopes and has nothing to do with planets.
protostar: A baby star still gathering material from its birth cloud, not yet fusing hydrogen.
pulsar: A rapidly spinning neutron star whose beams of radiation sweep past Earth as regular pulses.
red giant: A star that has swollen to a large size and cooled, glowing orange-red, late in its life.
reflection nebula: A cloud of gas and dust that shines by scattering the light of nearby stars, often looking bluish.
ring galaxy: A galaxy shaped like a ring, usually thought to form when a smaller galaxy plunges nearly head-on through a larger one and sends a wave of star formation outward.
RR Lyrae variable: An old pulsating star that brightens and dims in a cycle of about 0.2 to 1 day; RR Lyrae stars all have similar true brightness, so they serve as distance markers.
Seyfert galaxy: A galaxy, usually a spiral, with an exceptionally bright, star-like centre thought to be powered by a supermassive black hole; the most common and least energetic kind of active galaxy.
spectral type: A letter class, from hot O through B, A, F, G and K to cool M, that sorts stars by the lines in their light and so by their surface temperature.
spiral galaxy: A flat, rotating disk of stars, gas and dust with a central bulge and spiral arms, like a pinwheel.
starburst: A burst of star formation in a galaxy at a rate tens to hundreds of times higher than usual, often in its centre.
star cluster: A group of stars bound by gravity that formed together from the same cloud.
star-forming region: A part of a galaxy where a cloud of gas and dust is collapsing into new stars, often lit by the hot young ones.
supernova remnant: The expanding cloud of debris and swept-up gas left behind by an exploded star.
variable star: A star whose brightness changes over time, for example because the star itself pulsates or flares, or because a companion passes in front of it.
white dwarf: The small, hot, dense core left when a low- or medium-mass star has shed its outer layers and stopped fusing.
Wolf–Rayet star: A very hot, massive star that is blowing off its outer layers in a powerful wind, so its light shows broad emission lines.
grand-design spiral: A spiral galaxy whose arms are long, well defined and continuous, unlike patchy, fragmentary arms.
white dwarf cooling track: The path a white dwarf traces on a plot of brightness against temperature as it cools: with no fusion, it only radiates away stored heat, growing fainter and redder over billions of years.
luminous red nova: A red outburst that is typically brighter than a nova but fainter than a supernova, thought to come from two stars merging; it often brightens twice and stays bright for weeks to months.
polarimetry: Measuring the polarisation of light, the preferred direction in which its waves vibrate; it shows how the light was scattered or emitted, and so the make-up of its source.
Type Ia supernova: The explosion of a white dwarf that gains matter from a companion or merges with another white dwarf, which of the two is still debated; its spectrum shows no hydrogen, and because its peak brightness can be calibrated from how fast it fades, it is used to measure distances.
cometary knot: A dense knot of cool gas and dust at least twice the width of the Solar System, with a bright head facing the central star and a tail pointing away; the Helix Nebula holds thousands.
intracluster light: The faint glow of stars that belong to no single galaxy in a cluster but drift between its member galaxies.
H II region: A cloud of ionised hydrogen, often glowing red in the hydrogen-alpha line, lit by hot young stars whose ultraviolet light strips electrons from the gas; one lasts a few million years.
ionisation front: The boundary where ultraviolet light from hot stars turns neutral gas into ionised gas, moving outward through the surrounding cloud.
protostellar outflow: Gas ejected in two opposite jets or winds by a young star still gathering material; the jets move at up to several hundred km/s and push aside the slower gas of the cloud around them.
super star cluster: A young, very massive star cluster, with at least about 10,000 solar masses of stars, found where star formation is intense, as in galaxy mergers and starbursts; the biggest reach 100,000 solar masses or more.
tidal tail: A long, thin stream of stars and gas pulled out of a galaxy by the gravity of another galaxy passing close by.
supercluster: A huge, loose concentration of galaxy groups and clusters, typically tens of megaparsecs across.
void: A vast, nearly empty region of space between the filaments of galaxies, typically tens of megaparsecs across.
galaxy wall: A thin, sheet-like layer of galaxies stretching across hundreds of millions of light-years, such as the CfA2 Great Wall.
filament: A long thread of galaxies and gas, often tens of megaparsecs in length, that links galaxy clusters across the cosmic web.
galaxy cloud: A large clump of galaxies and groups within a supercluster, such as the Canes Venatici I Cloud in the Virgo Supercluster.
redshift: The stretching of light toward longer, redder wavelengths, caused by its source moving away from us or by the expansion of space.
peculiar velocity: The part of a galaxy's velocity left over after the smooth expansion of the universe is subtracted, caused by the gravitational pull of surrounding matter.
basin of attraction: The region of space whose galaxies all flow toward one common gravitational attractor, like water in a drainage basin.
zone of avoidance: The band of sky hidden behind the dust and stars of the Milky Way's disc, where distant galaxies are hard to see in visible light.
cosmic web: The largest pattern in the universe: galaxies and gas strung along filaments and sheets around nearly empty voids.
comoving distance: A distance measured on a grid that expands with the universe, so it stays fixed for galaxies carried along by the expansion; at the present time it equals the ordinary distance.
megaparsec: A unit of distance equal to one million parsecs, about 3.26 million light-years, used for distances between galaxies.
tip of the red giant branch: The brightness at which red giants stop getting brighter, a nearly constant value that astronomers use to measure the distance to a galaxy.
surface brightness fluctuations: A distance method that uses how grainy a galaxy looks: the star-to-star flicker in its glow fades with distance, so nearer galaxies look lumpier.
Local Void: A vast, nearly empty region of space next to the Local Group, away from which the Milky Way is moving.
kiloparsec: A unit of distance equal to 1,000 parsecs, about 3,260 light-years, used for sizes and distances within and around galaxies.
dwarf spheroidal galaxy: A small, faint, diffuse galaxy of mostly older stars with little or no gas, usually found near a larger galaxy and held together by a great deal of dark matter.
dwarf irregular galaxy: A small, gas-rich galaxy with no regular shape, usually still forming stars, with stars ranging from very old to newly born.
irregular galaxy: A galaxy with no regular shape, neither a spiral nor an elliptical, usually rich in gas and forming stars.
satellite galaxy: A smaller galaxy that circles a larger one, as the Magellanic Clouds circle the Milky Way; the host galaxy's gravity can stretch or tear it apart.
horizontal branch: The stage of old, low-mass stars that fuse helium in their cores after the red-giant stage; in metal-poor star clusters they form a nearly horizontal band of similar brightness on the colour-brightness diagram.
eclipsing binary: Two stars circling each other so that, seen from Earth, one regularly passes in front of the other and the light dips; the dips reveal the stars' sizes and, with their speeds, their masses.
period-luminosity relation: The link between how long a classical Cepheid takes to pulse and how bright it really is, found by Henrietta Leavitt: the slower the pulse, the brighter the star. It is used to measure distances; weaker versions exist for RR Lyrae stars and Miras.
velocity dispersion: The spread of the speeds of the stars in a galaxy or cluster around their average; if the system is in equilibrium, it measures the mass that holds it together.
mass-to-light ratio: The mass of an object divided by its luminosity, in solar units; stars alone give a few, so a far higher value means most of the mass gives off no light, pointing to dark matter.
Hubble flow: The motion of galaxies apart from one another that comes from the expansion of the universe alone, with a speed proportional to distance; it holds well beyond bound groups, where local motions add to it.
dark-matter halo: An extended cloud of dark matter around a galaxy, reaching far beyond its visible stars and holding most of its mass.
neutral hydrogen: Atomic hydrogen that has not lost its electron, written H I; it emits a faint radio line at 21 centimetres, with which astronomers map the gas in galaxies.
stellar stream: A long, thin trail of stars pulled out of a dwarf galaxy or star cluster by the tidal pull of a larger galaxy and stretched along the orbit of their source.
metal-poor: Having a much smaller share of elements heavier than helium (astronomers call them 'metals') than the Sun, as is typical of old stars and small galaxies.
metal-rich: Having a share of elements heavier than helium (astronomers call them 'metals') as high as the Sun's or higher, as in stars formed from gas enriched by earlier generations.
early-type galaxy: An elliptical or lenticular galaxy: smooth, without spiral arms, and made mostly of old red stars. 'Early' marks a place in the galaxy classification sequence, not youth.
late-type galaxy: A loosely wound spiral or irregular galaxy, typically blue and rich in gas and young stars. 'Late' marks a place in the galaxy classification sequence, not old age.
overdensity: A region where the density of galaxies or matter is higher than the cosmic average, usually given as how far above that average it is.
triaxial: Having three unequal axes, like a flattened, elongated ellipsoid rather than a sphere or a spheroid with a single axis of symmetry.
crossing time: The time a typical galaxy needs to cross a group or cluster at its usual speed; a system needs several crossing times to settle, so if it is longer than the age of the universe, the system cannot have settled into equilibrium.
dwarf elliptical galaxy: A small, smooth, faint galaxy of mostly older stars with little gas, brighter and denser than a dwarf spheroidal, often found beside a larger galaxy or in dense galaxy clusters.
potential well: A region of low gravitational potential around a concentration of mass, like a hollow that matter rolls into; the deeper the well, the more energy it takes to climb out.
watershed: A boundary where flows part in opposite directions, as water does at a ridge; in Laniakea's definition, where galaxies' motions diverge toward different gravitational centres.
repeller: A region, usually a big void, that is emptier than its surroundings, so nearby matter is pulled less toward it than away from it and seems to flow away; the opposite of an attractor.
tidal stream: A long, thin stream of stars pulled out of a dwarf galaxy or star cluster by the tidal pull of a larger galaxy, stretched out roughly along the orbit of the original object.
comoving coordinates: Positions measured on a grid that expands with the universe, so galaxies carried along by the expansion keep the same coordinates; at the present time they match ordinary distances.
main sequence: The long stage in which a star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core; on a plot of brightness against colour, such stars form a band, and most stars, the Sun included, are on it.
stellar population: A group of stars that share an origin and chemical make-up. Globular clusters often hold more than one, told apart by their abundances of elements such as nitrogen, sodium and oxygen, or by separate sequences in a brightness-colour diagram.
anemic spiral: A spiral galaxy with unusually little star formation for its type: its arms are smooth and low in contrast, often because it has lost or used up much of its gas.
flocculent spiral: A spiral galaxy whose arms are patchy, short and low in contrast instead of two long, continuous arms.
millisecond pulsar: A pulsar that spins once every few milliseconds: an old neutron star spun up by gas falling in from a companion star.
core-collapsed cluster: A globular cluster whose centre has contracted into an unusually dense knot of stars, after its heavier stars sank inward and the core lost energy.
galactic wind: A flow of gas blown out of a galaxy by the radiation and supernova explosions of its young stars.
OB association: A loose group of young, massive stars of spectral types O and B that formed together but are no longer held by gravity and slowly drift apart.
metallicity: The share of a star's or galaxy's matter made of elements heavier than helium, which astronomers call metals; old stars usually have low metallicity.
